passage:
Mahima, sit. You asked why your Deepak Mama went quiet at the sweet shop just now. Let me tell you.
When I was nineteen, my Amma died in the April of my second year. By October I thought I was fine. Marks were back up, I was laughing in the canteen again. Then one morning in the chemistry lecture, someone behind me opened a tiffin of besan laddoos. Amma's Diwali smell, cardamom and roasted gram flour. My eyes just flooded. I had to walk out with the whole class staring.
I sat on the stairs thinking, six months of progress, gone. I was so ashamed.
It took me years to understand I hadn't slipped back at all. Grief moves like the tide, beta. It goes out, it comes in, and the coming in doesn't cancel the going out. Today at the shop was just another wave.

qa.q: What smell set off Deepak's tears in the chemistry lecture?
qa.a: Besan laddoos from a tiffin behind him, Amma's Diwali smell of cardamom and roasted gram flour.

qa.q: What did nineteen-year-old Deepak think and feel as he sat on the stairs?
qa.a: He thought six months of progress were gone and felt ashamed, as if the sudden tears meant he had gone backwards.

qa.q: What could have helped Deepak on those stairs that day?
qa.a: Knowing that grief comes in waves would have let him see the tears as a normal surge rather than a failure, and he could have told a friend what the smell had stirred.

qa.q: How might a classmate in that chemistry lecture have seen Deepak walking out?
qa.a: A classmate might have been confused or worried, seeing only sudden tears and not knowing that the smell of the laddoos had brought back Amma's death.

grounding: Shows a sudden wave of grief triggered by a festival smell in a lecture hall, and the false feeling of having gone backwards.

The client call was in ten minutes, and Hansa's slides still had a typo on page four. Then the pantry speaker, playing someone's old-songs list, started the harmonium opening of the ghazal her Papa used to hum while shaving.
Seven months, and she had not cried at work once. Now her eyes spilled over before she could stop them. She stood frozen at the whiteboard, marker in hand, thinking, I was doing so well. Why now?
Arohi, from the next desk, glanced over and quietly turned the speaker down. "Want me to open the call while you wash your face?"
Hansa nodded. In the washroom she pressed a wet tissue to her eyes and whispered, "Seven months," as though the number should have protected her.
Four minutes later she walked back in, fixed the typo and unmuted, still not sure what had just happened to her.

qa.q: What was Hansa's Papa's ghazal played on?
qa.a: It came on the pantry speaker, playing someone's old-songs list.

qa.q: What does Hansa's thought 'I was doing so well. Why now?' suggest she believes?
qa.a: She feels shaken and discouraged, as if one sudden wave of tears after seven months undoes all her progress.

qa.q: What could help Hansa once the client call is over?
qa.a: She could remind herself that grief returns in waves, tell Arohi what the song meant, and expect that other reminders like it may come.

qa.q: How might Arohi have read the moment at the whiteboard?
qa.a: Arohi saw a colleague frozen in tears just before a deadline and chose small, practical help, turning the music down and offering to open the call, without asking for explanations.

grounding: Illustrates a song unexpectedly bringing tears at the office months after a death, and the surprise of the wave feeling like a setback.
